Every graph in CausalStructures precomputes and stores each node's parents,
children, spouses, and neighbors directly, so `parents()`, `children()`,
`spouses()`, and `neighbors()` are effectively $O(1)$ lookups rather than scans
over the whole edge set. Many higher-level algorithms, including
`d_separated()`/`m_separated()`, `minimal_separator()`, and adjustment-set
search, are built on these primitive operations, so their performance depends
directly on the efficiency of these basic queries.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(CausalStructures)

# The median time of each expression. Memory allocated inside the library, and
# its garbage collection, is invisible to bench, so only the time is shown.
timings <- function(..., iterations = 200) {
  b <- bench::mark(..., iterations = iterations, check = FALSE)
  data.frame(expression = names(b$expression), median = format(b$median))
}
```

## Queries stay fast as graphs grow

Single-hop queries such as `children()` are just slice lookups, so their runtime
is essentially unchanged whether the graph has 100 nodes or 10,000:

```{r}
graphs <- lapply(c(100, 1000, 10000), \(n) {
  generate_graph(n, p = 5 / n, seed = 1)
})
timings(
  "n = 100" = children(graphs[[1]], "V50"),
  "n = 1,000" = children(graphs[[2]], "V500"),
  "n = 10,000" = children(graphs[[3]], "V5000")
)
```

These primitives keep more involved queries fast too, on graphs with hundreds of
nodes and across graph classes:

```{r}
dag <- generate_graph(500, p = 0.1, seed = 1)
mag <- generate_graph(500, p = 0.01, class = "MAG", latents = 20, seed = 1)
x <- "V10"
y <- "V290"

timings(
  "d_separated (DAG)" = d_separated(dag, x, y),
  "m_separated (MAG)" = m_separated(mag, x, y),
  "topological_sort" = topological_sort(dag),
  "minimal_separator" = minimal_separator(dag, x, y),
  "markov_blanket" = markov_blanket(dag, x)
)
```

## Searching for adjustment sets

`all_backdoor_sets()`, `all_adjustment_sets()`, `all_iv_sets()`, and
`all_frontdoor_sets()` search subsets of the candidate universe up to
`max_size`, checking each one against the relevant validity criterion.
Consequently, the runtime grows exponentially with `max_size`:

```{r}
admg <- generate_graph(35, p = 0.15, class = "ADMG", latents = 8, seed = 1)
x <- "V3"
y <- "V33"

sizes <- 2:4
n_sets <- vapply(
  sizes,
  \(ms) length(all_adjustment_sets(admg, x, y, minimal = FALSE, max_size = ms)),
  integer(1)
)
cbind(
  timings(
    "max_size = 2" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 2
    ),
    "max_size = 3" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 3
    ),
    "max_size = 4" = all_adjustment_sets(
      admg,
      x,
      y,
      minimal = FALSE,
      max_size = 4
    ),
    iterations = 20
  ),
  sets = n_sets
)
```

## Expensive algorithms

Here we will show the performance of some of the most expensive algorithms.

### Exact uniform DAG sampling

`generate_graph()` uses an Erdős--Rényi model: it samples each edge
independently, which is cheap regardless of `n` but is not uniform over the
space of DAGs. `uniform_dag()` instead draws exactly uniformly from all labeled
DAGs on `n` nodes using the recursive enumeration algorithm of
@kuipers2015uniform:[^counts]

```{r}
timings(
  "n = 10" = uniform_dag(10, seed = 1),
  "n = 20" = uniform_dag(20, seed = 1),
  "n = 40" = uniform_dag(40, seed = 1),
  iterations = 20
)
```

[^counts]: Each call in this benchmark computes the counting table from scratch.
    In practice, when drawing several DAGs on `n` or fewer nodes, compute the
    table once with `uniform_dag_counts(n)` and pass it to every call as
    `counts`.

### Markov equivalence class enumeration

`count_dags()` and `enumerate_dags()` operate on a CPDAG, PDAG, or MPDAG by
considering every DAG in its Markov equivalence class. The size of that class
grows combinatorially with the number of undirected edges. For example, a clique
on $k$ nodes has $k!$ consistent orientations, so the class can grow very large
very quickly:

```{r}
# A PDAG whose k nodes are all joined by undirected edges
clique <- function(k) {
  pairs <- utils::combn(paste0("V", seq_len(k)), 2)
  cgraph(
    spec = paste(pairs[1, ], "---", pairs[2, ], collapse = ", "),
    class = "PDAG"
  )
}
cliques <- lapply(c(5, 7, 8), clique)
vapply(cliques, count_dags, numeric(1))

timings(
  "count_dags, k = 5" = count_dags(cliques[[1]]),
  "count_dags, k = 7" = count_dags(cliques[[2]]),
  "count_dags, k = 8" = count_dags(cliques[[3]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 5" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[1]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 7" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[2]]),
  "enumerate_dags, k = 8" = enumerate_dags(cliques[[3]]),
  iterations = 5
)
```

`enumerate_dags()` must materialize every DAG rather than simply count them, so
it is slower and uses more memory than `count_dags()`, as the numbers above
show. In R, every DAG it returns is also a `cgraph`, so keep the class small, or
use `count_dags()` first to check its size.

### MAG equivalence class enumeration

`enumerate_mags()` is the PAG/MAG counterpart to `enumerate_dags()`. While
`enumerate_dags()` is fairly efficient via Chickering's recursive pruning,
`enumerate_mags()` simply brute-forces every tail/arrowhead assignment for each
circle endpoint in the PAG ($2^k$ candidates for $k$ circle endpoints), and
keeps the candidates that are valid MAGs with the given PAG as their equivalence
class. Thus, it's considerably more expensive than
`count_dags()`/`enumerate_dags()`:

```{r}
# A PAG whose k nodes are all joined by o-o edges
circle_clique <- function(k) {
  pairs <- utils::combn(paste0("V", seq_len(k)), 2)
  cgraph(
    spec = paste(pairs[1, ], "o-o", pairs[2, ], collapse = ", "),
    class = "PAG"
  )
}
pags <- lapply(3:4, circle_clique)
vapply(pags, \(pag) length(enumerate_mags(pag)), integer(1))

timings(
  "k = 3" = enumerate_mags(pags[[1]]),
  "k = 4" = enumerate_mags(pags[[2]]),
  iterations = 5
)
```

With one more node, `k = 5`, the class has 4,457 MAGs among $2^{20}$ candidates,
and `enumerate_mags()` takes tens of seconds.

::: {.callout-tip title="Parallel search"}
`count_dags()`, `enumerate_dags()`, `enumerate_mags()`, `pagcauses()`, and the
whole `all_*_sets()` family[^1] parallelize their search across the library's
threads automatically once the problem is large enough to benefit. The library
runs with one thread unless the `JULIA_NUM_THREADS` environment variable (a
number, or `"auto"` for one per core) is set before the package is loaded, e.g.
in your `.Renviron`.

[^1]: Except for `all_iv_sets()`, since the candidate check for IV is a trivial
    lookup, and thus not worth it.
:::
